ComprehensionText:
Give the Tricksters Their Due
Ask most students to name a character from mythology and you will probably hear about a hero: Hercules wrestling a lion, perhaps, or Perseus with his mirrored shield. Heroes dominate the posters, the films and the school units. I think that is a pity, because the most useful characters in the world's myths are not the heroes at all. They are the tricksters, and it is time they were given a proper place in our classrooms.
A trickster is a clever, mischievous figure who wins by wit rather than strength. Almost every culture has one. In West Africa and the Caribbean, Anansi the spider outwits creatures far larger than himself. In Polynesian stories, Maui snares the sun with ropes and slows it down so that his people have longer days. In Norse myth, Loki stirs up chaos and then, as often as not, has to fix it. North American peoples tell of Coyote, and Japanese folktales feature a shape-shifting fox. The fact that so many cultures, separated by oceans, created such similar characters should make us curious. They must be telling us something people everywhere needed to hear.
So what do tricksters teach? First, they show that brains can beat brawn. Most of us will never wrestle a lion, but all of us will face problems that need creative solutions. A hero's answer is usually to be stronger; a trickster's answer is to think differently. That is a lesson worth more than any amount of sword-swinging.
Second, tricksters are honest about failure. Heroes rarely make mistakes, which makes them hard to relate to. Tricksters, on the other hand, are forever getting caught in their own traps. Anansi's greed lands him in trouble again and again. Readers laugh, but they also learn that cleverness without good judgement can backfire. I can think of no better lesson for a teenager.
Third, trickster tales are funny, and humour is a powerful aid to memory. Students who yawn through a list of ancient kings will happily retell the story of how a spider persuaded a python to stretch out beside a branch to settle an argument about its length, then tied it up.
Some people argue that tricksters are poor role models because they lie and cheat. I understand the worry, but it misreads the stories. Nobody finishes an Anansi tale wanting to copy his greed; they finish it understanding where greed leads. Myths have never been simple instruction manuals. They are invitations to think.
I am not asking schools to throw out Hercules. Heroes have their place, and their courage is worth admiring. But if we only ever teach the strong, we send students the message that problems are solved by force and that winners are people who never stumble. The tricksters tell a truer story: that the small can outsmart the mighty, that mistakes are part of learning, and that a good laugh can carry wisdom across a thousand years. Let's give them their due.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Water Uphill to Kalgoorlie
In 1892, prospectors found gold at Coolgardie, in the dry country more than five hundred kilometres east of Perth. A year later, an Irish prospector named Paddy Hannan made another find nearby, at what became Kalgoorlie. Tens of thousands of people rushed to the area hoping to make their fortunes. They found gold, but they also found one of the harshest environments in Australia. Rain was scarce and unreliable, there were no permanent rivers, and the little groundwater available was often too salty to drink.
Water quickly became more precious than the gold itself. It was carted in on camels, collected in tanks, or produced by condensers that boiled salty water and captured the steam. In hot summers, a bucket of water could cost more than a meal. Without clean water, diseases such as typhoid spread through the crowded camps, and many people died.
The government of Western Australia turned to its Engineer-in-Chief, Charles Yelverton O'Connor, who had already built the harbour at Fremantle. His plan was astonishing for its time. He proposed building a dam on the Helena River in the hills near Perth and pumping water through a pipeline about 530 kilometres long to the goldfields. The difficulty was not only the distance. Kalgoorlie stands about 400 metres higher than the dam, so the water would have to be pushed uphill most of the way.
Many people thought the idea was impossible or wasteful. Newspapers mocked it, and some politicians argued that the gold might run out before the pipeline was finished, leaving the colony with an enormous debt and a pipe to nowhere. O'Connor and the Premier, John Forrest, held firm, and work began in 1898.
The project used new technology. Instead of riveting the steel pipes, engineers used a locking-bar method that clamped the edges of each pipe together, making the joints stronger and less likely to leak. Thousands of workers laid the pipes in the summer heat, and eight steam-driven pumping stations were built along the route to lift the water in stages.
In January 1903, the water reached Kalgoorlie, and crowds celebrated as it gushed into a reservoir on the edge of town. O'Connor did not see that day. He died in 1902, less than a year before the opening, after years of fierce public criticism. Today he is remembered as one of the country's great engineers.
The goldfields boomed after the water arrived. Towns gained gardens, parks and swimming pools, and the mining industry could expand with confidence. The pipeline, later extended to farms and towns across the Wheatbelt, still operates more than a century later, though electric pumps have replaced the old steam engines. In 2009 it was recognised as an International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark, an honour it shares with structures such as the Eiffel Tower and the Panama Canal.
The pipeline changed what people believed was possible in the Australian interior. It showed that, with enough vision and determination, even a desert town could be given a reliable supply of water.

Teaching Your Budgie to Step Up
Budgerigars, or budgies, are small Australian parrots that have become one of the most popular pets in the world. In the wild they fly in large, chattering flocks across the inland, so a single budgie in a cage can easily become bored and lonely. Training is one of the best ways to keep a pet budgie's mind busy, and the first skill most owners teach is the 'step up', in which the bird hops onto your finger when asked. This guide explains how to teach it safely.
What you will need
- a quiet room with the windows and doors closed and any ceiling fans switched off
- a supply of millet spray, a seed treat most budgies adore
- a short, smooth perch or a clean wooden chopstick
- patience: some birds learn in a week, while others take a month or more
Before you begin
A budgie brought home from a pet shop or breeder needs time to settle. For at least the first week, do not try to handle it. Instead, sit beside the cage each day and talk softly so the bird grows used to your voice and presence. Budgies are prey animals, and in the wild a shape swooping from above could mean a hungry hawk. Rushing this stage can leave a bird nervous of hands for life.
Step 1: Hand in the cage
Rest your hand quietly inside the cage, near but not touching the bird, for a few minutes at a time. Hold a piece of millet between your fingers. At first your budgie may flutter away, but over several sessions it will usually edge closer to nibble the treat. Do not grab at it.
Step 2: Offer a finger
Once your budgie eats calmly from your hand, slide one finger slowly towards it, just above its feet. Approach from the side or below, never from directly overhead. Say 'step up' in a clear, cheerful tone as you press very gently against its lower chest. Most budgies will lift a foot to keep their balance. The moment both feet are on your finger, reward the bird with millet and praise.
Step 3: Practise and progress
Keep sessions short, about five to ten minutes, and finish while your budgie is still keen. A tired or frightened bird will start to puff, pant or flap, which is a sign to stop. Repeat the command using exactly the same words each time. When your budgie steps up reliably inside the cage, you can try carrying it a short distance out of the cage.
Troubleshooting
If your bird bites, do not jerk your hand away, as this teaches it that biting works. Hold still, stay calm and try again later. If your budgie is afraid of fingers, offer the perch or chopstick instead; many birds feel safer stepping onto wood. If your budgie seems uninterested, try a session shortly before its usual feeding time, when a millet reward will seem far more tempting.
A well-trained budgie is a happier, more confident companion. The chirps and chatter you hear at the end of a successful session are your reward for all that patience.

Training is one of the best ways to keep a pet budgie's mind busy, and the first skill most owners teach is the 'step up', in which the bird hops onto your finger when asked. This guide explains how to teach it safely.
What you will need
- a quiet room with the windows and doors closed and any ceiling fans switched off
- a supply of millet spray, a seed treat most budgies adore
- a short, smooth perch or a clean wooden chopstick
- patience: some birds learn in a week, while others take a month or more
Before you begin
A budgie brought home from a pet shop or breeder needs time to settle. For at least the first week, do not try to handle it. Instead, sit beside the cage each day and talk softly so the bird grows used to your voice and presence. Budgies are prey animals, and in the wild a shape swooping from above could mean a hungry hawk. Rushing this stage can leave a bird nervous of hands for life.
Step 1: Hand in the cage
Rest your hand quietly inside the cage, near but not touching the bird, for a few minutes at a time. Hold a piece of millet between your fingers. At first your budgie may flutter away, but over several sessions it will usually edge closer to nibble the treat. Do not grab at it.
Step 2: Offer a finger
Once your budgie eats calmly from your hand, slide one finger slowly towards it, just above its feet. Approach from the side or below, never from directly overhead. Say 'step up' in a clear, cheerful tone as you press very gently against its lower chest. Most budgies will lift a foot to keep their balance. The moment both feet are on your finger, reward the bird with millet and praise.
Step 3: Practise and progress
Keep sessions short, about five to ten minutes, and finish while your budgie is still keen. A tired or frightened bird will start to puff, pant or flap, which is a sign to stop. Repeat the command using exactly the same words each time. When your budgie steps up reliably inside the cage, you can try carrying it a short distance out of the cage.
Troubleshooting
If your bird bites, do not jerk your hand away, as this teaches it that biting works. Hold still, stay calm and try again later. If your budgie is afraid of fingers, offer the perch or chopstick instead; many birds feel safer stepping onto wood. If your budgie seems uninterested, try a session shortly before its usual feeding time, when a millet reward will seem far more tempting.
A well-trained budgie is a happier, more confident companion. The chirps and chatter you hear at the end of a successful session are your reward for all that patience.

The first thing Jaya learned at the Westside Community Kitchen was that Mr Okafor did not say hello. He looked up from the stove when she came through the back door on Saturday morning, glanced at her new apron, and pointed his wooden spoon at a sack in the corner.
'Onions,' he said. 'Forty. Diced.'
Jaya had signed up because her school required twenty hours of community service, and the kitchen was the only place within walking distance of home. Her mother had laughed when she heard. 'You? In a kitchen? You burn toast.' She had imagined serving meals with a friendly smile, not crying over a chopping board while a man with a grey beard ignored her.
By the sixth onion, her eyes were streaming and her pieces were all different sizes. Mr Okafor came over, took one look and swept the whole pile into a bowl.
'Stock,' he said. 'Start again.'
Jaya felt her face go hot. She nearly untied her apron there and then. Instead, she grabbed another onion and attacked it, harder this time, determined not to give him the satisfaction of seeing her quit.
'Stop.' He was beside her again. This time he did not take the board away. He put his large hand over hers and tilted the knife so the tip rested on the board. 'You are chopping like you are angry with it. The onion has done nothing to you. Rock the blade. Let the knife do the work. Curl your fingers, so.' He showed her, his knuckles guiding the side of the blade. 'Cut the root last. The root holds it together, and it holds the tears in too.'
She tried it. The slices came out thin and even. He grunted, which she would later learn was the closest he came to praise, and went back to his pot.
Mr Okafor did not look at her again, but when she reached for the next onion, he slid a bowl of cold water along the bench. 'Wet the knife,' he said. 'Helps.'
By the twentieth onion, she had found a rhythm. By the thirtieth, her eyes had almost stopped stinging. By the fortieth, the smell of onions softening in oil filled the hall, and people had begun to line up outside.
At noon, Jaya stood at the serving table beside a woman named Rosa, who had volunteered every Saturday for nine years. Jaya's arms ached and her apron smelt of onion, but she found she didn't mind.
'He made me do the onions too,' Rosa said, ladling stew into a bowl. 'Everyone does the onions on their first day. Half of them never come back.'
'Why does he do it?'
Rosa shrugged. 'He says if you can't be patient with an onion, you won't be patient with people.' She nodded at the queue, where an elderly man was slowly counting out coins he did not need to pay. 'And people here need patience more than anything.'
Jaya watched the man carry his bowl to a corner table and close his eyes as the steam rose into his face. Somewhere in that stew were her forty onions.
The following Saturday, she arrived ten minutes early. Mr Okafor looked up from the stove, glanced at her apron, and almost smiled.
'Carrots,' he said.
QuestionText: Why did Jaya sign up to volunteer at the kitchen?
AnswerA: She wanted to learn to cook for her family.
AnswerB: Her friend Rosa had asked her to help.
AnswerC: Her school required community service hours.
AnswerD: Mr Okafor had offered her a paid job.

A Lasting Impact Scarlett looked on with pride as she observed a fellow eighth grader casually walk over to one of the many recycling bins at school to dispose of an empty water bottle. As the new president of the school recycling club, Scarlett had played a big part in increasing awareness about the importance of recycling items properly. She and the other members of the club had worked together to make sure that a recycling bin was in every public area at the school. "A simple action that has a lasting impact" was the slogan the members of the recycling club had placed on each bin, reminding students that disposing of recyclable items was an easy task that could have a profound effect on the environment. The school year had just begun, and Scarlett was already thinking about activities to encourage students to be more enthusiastic about recycling. As the president of the recycling club, she wanted to surpass the recycling record the school had set the previous year. The school had recycled an amazing amount of trash for the past five years, and she hoped this year would be even better. Scarlett went home at the end of the day, feeling optimistic about the school year. She sat down at her computer and looked online, hoping to find inspiration for events the club could organize at school. Instead, she uncovered some alarming information that quickly swept away her positive attitude. During her research, she learned that electronic waste, or e-waste as it is commonly called, represents about 2 percent of trash in landfills. No-longer-used computers, cell phones, and televisions are just a few examples of this type of waste. Unfortunately, as companies that produce these items continue to improve upon technology and people replace existing electronics with newer, better versions, the amount of e-waste that is created will only increase. Scarlett was disappointed in herself for not taking action to bring awareness to this problem sooner. At that moment, she began to develop a plan. The next day at school, Scarlett was on a mission. There was one person who would definitely be able to help the recycling club bring attention to this cause. "Hey, Juan Carlos," Scarlett beamed as she saw her friend in the hallway. "How would you like to make your last year of middle school a real success?" Juan Carlos gave a questioning look before Scarlett outlined her plan.
